doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: The 1973 Charlie Parker Festival
summary: The week-long festival on KCR, Tristano's network of listeners, and hearing it in the streets.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Oh yeah, yeah. I can’t now, it’s just a joke now. But Tristano recognized the significance of the Charlie Parker festival and started a musician’s network largely of his students telephoning and he single handedly in this regard, probably added ten to twenty thousand listeners of a devout nature to the KCR experiment, because of our week-long celebration of Charlie Parker in August and September of 1973. At the time, when I was at Columbia — I had graduated by this time — but when I was at Columbia my day gig was in the ID office. I did refereeing and the day gig. The ID office became my proverbial day gig to pay for my jazz life until August of 1980. For seven years that’s how I paid my bills. So and it was registration for the fall semester of ’73 at Columbia University while the Charlie Parker festival is going on. And there used to be a fire exit we used to walk out of the back door to quickly hit the street from KCR. So I dropped the record and it was “Scrapple from the Apple,” the C take, November 4, ’47. And it’s on the air and it’s like that’s the record I love. My mother’s favorite Charlie Parker record and Ben Webster’s favorite Charlie Parker record so there you have it. But the record’s grooving me and I’m thinking about it and hearing it and then I leave the station, I hit the fire exit and the record is gone. But the record is still in my brain because I’m playing it in my brain. And then I hit the street and the record was back, not just in my brain. This was very hot, it was summer and air conditioning wasn’t so endemic. So people had their windows open and they were playing the Charlie Parker festival on the radio. I said, “We hit the jackpot.” And then there was a guy from WABC — are you running out of time here with your film guy?

WABC — Steven K. Nenno was his name. So the Charlie Parker Festival, this is the turning point of KCR. I started February 2, of ’70. I’m doing what I did already. But only a few people are listening. One of them is Tristano and he calls up to yell at me. But then I did the Charlie Parker Festival. Or really Irv Schenkler did the Charlie Parker Festival using my Charlie Parker chops. I’m the guy, he’s the producer. That’s a fair operation. And Tristano says, “Phil got the right idea.” And so he calls the studio and says, “I’m calling you, you call five people I don’t know.” And then by whatever it was, I was sitting on a park bench with Howard McGhee on August 30, 1973 and we’re listening to the Charlie Parker Festival eating ice cream.
